claims.text: The starting high-entropy alloy is largely disordered in its as-cast state, with a random distribution of constituent atoms.
Controlled low-temperature in situ annealing will promote slight local ordering in the alloy.
The emergence of superconductivity is governed by nanoscale regions with enhanced short-range crystalline order.
Locally ordered domains promote stronger electron-phonon coupling.
Local structural ordering decreases electron scattering.
Enhanced local electron-phonon coupling facilitates Cooper-pair formation and the opening of a superconducting gap.
A global superconducting state is established when locally superconducting regions reach a percolation threshold.
The annealed sample will have a more spatially uniform superconducting-gap distribution than the untreated sample.
A larger fraction of regions in the annealed sample will display a clear superconducting gap.
Spatial superconducting-gap uniformity will correlate with short-range order observed by local structural imaging.
The untreated as-cast baseline has spatially heterogeneous or absent superconducting-gap signals.
The proposed mechanism applies to HEAs with similar compositional balances at temperatures below 10 K.
The proposed effect will be limited if the alloy remains completely disordered.
Inducing long-range rather than nanoscale order may alter the superconducting behavior entirely.
The fraction and size of ordered regions required for global superconductivity are unknown.
The comparison will keep overall alloy composition constant and use an untreated sample as the control.
Failure to observe a statistically significant ordering-correlated increase in homogeneous gaps, or a corresponding change in global Tc, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as 'largely disordered,' whereas the baseline calls the same as-cast state 'fully disordered.'
